An Analysis of Sleep, Exercise Behaviour, and Active Calories Burnt

What Are We Talking About Today?

As I am approaching an old age (24), my body has felt the importance of the presence, and, absence of sleep.

Adequate sleep, or the lack of sleep will affect how we feel the next day, the exercise level our body endures, leading to how much calories we burn. In this report we will explore how sleep affects exercise behaviours and the active calories burnt.

A brown monkey lying down on white pillow covered in whie blacket on white sheets. The monkey extends it’s right arm out onto the grey mouse pad of a grey laptop with black keyboards. The monkey is looking in the direction of the laptop.

Sleep patterns across weekdays and weekends

The sleep patterns differ between weekdays and weekends:

Weekdays show a strong concentration in “Moderate (6–8 hours)” sleep
Weekends show more variability, with higher representation of both:
- “A lot (More than 10 hours)”
- “Low sleep consistency categories”

This suggests that sleep is more structured during weekdays, while weekends introduce irregular sleep recovery behaviour (probably because there’s more time to have fun during the weekend)

Exercise Level and Energy Output

There is a clear relationship between exercise duration and calories burned:

High exercise duration (Over 30 minutes) leads to the highest average calorie burn
No exercise (0 minutes) corresponds to the lowest calorie output
The increase is gradual, suggesting a dose–response relationship between exercise and energy expenditure

This confirms that even moderate increases in exercise time can meaningfully impact daily calorie burn

Activity Trends Over Time

Calorie burn fluctuates significantly across time:

  • There are noticeable spikes in activity, likely reflecting active days
  • Some periods show low and stable energy expenditure, indicating rest or low-activity days
  • The pattern suggests a non-linear lifestyle rhythm, rather than consistent daily activity (I am unemployed and I don’t have a consistent schedule. I am sedentary whenever I want and active whenever I want)

This variability highlights how daily behaviour changes rather than remaining stable

Sleep vs Calories Burnt Relationship

Sleep duration appears to influence energy levels:

  • Observations with moderate sleep (6–8 hours) show a wide range of calorie burnt values
  • Very low sleep groups show less consistent activity patterns
  • Higher sleep categories do not necessarily guarantee higher or lower calorie burn, but they show greater variability and some higher outliers

This suggests sleep affects energy, but the relationship is not strictly linear.

- The weekdays are more structured in both sleep and activity
